source: Fu, Vanek & Roberts (2023/2024) Matched or moved? Asymmetry in high- and low-level visual processing of motion events (Lang Cogn 16:283-306), Exp 1 b-CFS
finding: Partial replication of an earlier N=24/group study (Vanek & Fu 2023) at about twice the size. English speakers detected manner-different motion faster than Mandarin speakers when the video broke through continuous flash suppression, with no speech task. This is a manner effect before any language use. It is not the Papafragou gaze-timing paradigm.
numbers: Exp 1 recruited 55 Mandarin and 52 English speakers (a few excluded for accuracy). Condition x Language interaction beta=-0.18, SE=0.06, t=-2.854, p=0.004. English: manner-mismatch RTs shorter than path-mismatch (t=-2.82, p=0.006). Mandarin: manner vs path mismatch beta=0.03, t=0.48, p=0.63.
limits: Not a speaking task; logRT mixed models; recruited samples, not a preregistered replication of 2008. Authors note linguistic modulation is often transient.
agent_relevance: Closest thing found to a 50+ per group conceptual extension for gap 2. Suggests label-driven salience can act automatically, which is the strong reading of thinking for speaking. No direct test of agent behaviour.

source: Fu, Vanek & Roberts (2023/2024), Exp 2 sentence-video verification
finding: When language is overt (a sentence is read, then a video is verified) the pattern changes: English speakers were slower for manner mismatches than for path mismatches, Mandarin speakers showed no manner/path difference. The authors call this an asymmetry between detecting contrasts (low level) and verifying matches (high level).
numbers: 51 Mandarin and 51 English speakers recruited. Mandarin manner vs path mismatch beta=0.064, SE=0.1, t=0.64, p=0.524. English full mismatch faster than manner mismatch (beta=-0.49, t=-4.00, p<0.001) and than path mismatch (beta=-0.23, t=-2.13, p=0.039).
limits: Direction depends on task; the authors offer a recency account and a predictive processing account. One lab, one language pair.
agent_relevance: The same language difference can speed or slow responses depending on whether labels are used to detect or to verify. A scaffold step that primes labels may help one operation and hurt another.

source: Soroli (2024) How language influences spatial thinking, categorization of motion events, and gaze behavior: a cross-linguistic comparison (Lang Cogn 16(4))
finding: English vs French (satellite- vs verb-framed) speakers did three eye-tracking tasks. In a NON-verbal categorisation task French speakers chose path-congruent variants more often than English speakers. In a verbal similarity task the gap grew. Production differences were called massive. Gaze effects were partial and depended on event type and scene type.
numbers: 20 speakers per language per experiment analysed (49 tested, 40 kept). Non-verbal: French 78% path-congruent vs English 59% (English 41% manner). Verbal: English 67% manner vs French 41% manner; language effect F(1,36)=16.71, p<0.001. Manner choices rose from non-verbal to verbal in both groups (French F(1,18)=26.14; English F(1,18)=31.30; both p<0.001).
limits: N=20 per cell. Included artificial and cartoon scenes that the author says raise language effects. The non-verbal effect conflicts with the null non-verbal results of Papafragou 2008 and Lee et al. 2026; no verbal interference was used.
agent_relevance: Graded picture: language involvement raises the effect, but a small effect may remain without speaking. For an agent, treat description-language effects as strongest right after a describing step.

source: Athanasopoulos & Bylund (2013) Does grammatical aspect affect motion event cognition? (as described in Fu et al. 2023)
finding: Second-hand through an opened paper. Four experiments with English (aspect grammaticalised) and Swedish (not) speakers. Groups differed when describing endpoint-biased and ongoing events and in memory-based similarity judgements under high task demand. Differences vanished in an online similarity task and in a memory task with verbal interference.
numbers: No statistics in the secondary text; original paper not opened.
limits: Second-hand only. Exact figures still needed; gap 8 stays open for numbers.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition in one study: the aspect effect lives where language can be used as a strategy and dies under verbal interference. Same pattern as Gennari 2002.

source: Ji (2017) and Flecken et al. (2015) as described in Fu et al. (2023)
finding: Second-hand. Ji 2017: Chinese and English speakers picked path-sharing pairs more often, but English speakers were faster for manner matches, and this survived number repetition. Flecken et al. 2015 (EEG): German speakers' brain responses were more sensitive to endpoints, English speakers' to trajectories.
numbers: No numbers in the secondary text.
limits: Second-hand. Ji 2017 did not specify the language of the number distracters, which weakens the 'automatic' reading.
agent_relevance: With d01 this is the main case that language effects may be automatic. Open, not settled.

source: Gennari, Sloman, Malt & Fitch (2002) Motion events in language and cognition (Cognition 83:49-79), introduction describing Slobin
finding: Page-level description of Slobin's evidence. Slobin (1996a,b, 1997) analysed Spanish-English translations, narrations from the same pictures, and mental images linked to narrations. He found manner verbs more numerous in English and a more elaborated manner vocabulary. Slobin proposes English speakers habitually attend to manner and find it more codable. Gennari et al. point out that every response pattern in these studies is itself linguistic, so it cannot show non-linguistic effects.
numbers: Gennari's own data: see a10, b05, b06 in earlier evidence files.
quote: Slobin argues that language may have an effect mainly on the processes of thinking for speaking
limits: This is Gennari et al.'s reading of Slobin, not Slobin 1996 itself (never opened; publisher pages blocked). Berman & Slobin 1994 numbers not obtained.
agent_relevance: Clarifies the claim: Slobin's evidence shows language-shaped speaking, and the cognitive claim is a hypothesis about attention during production. Agent analogue is output-format pressure on what gets attended during planning.

source: Papafragou, Hulbert & Trueswell (2008) introduction, how thinking for speaking is framed (PMC2810627)
finding: The paper states the idea as: obligatory distinctions make message formulation automatic and shape utterance preparation before specific words are chosen. It cites Slobin 1996, 2003. It reports that Path vs Manner differences in how children talk about motion are in place by about age 3 (Slobin 1996, 2003; contested by Naigles et al. 1998 and Papafragou et al. 2002, 2006). It quotes Slobin 2004 that manner is a salient and differentiated conceptual field for Manner-language speakers.
numbers: No new numbers; Berman & Slobin 1994 frog-story rates by age not given in this source.
limits: Secondary description of Slobin. Developmental frog-story figures for manner and path by language and age remain unobtained.
agent_relevance: Confirms what to test in an agent: does a required output form change what is encoded before wording starts.

source: Search note: Slobin (1996) and Berman & Slobin (1994) page-level access
finding: Could not open Slobin 1996 (Rethinking Linguistic Relativity chapter) or Berman & Slobin 1994. Publisher and repository pages returned 403, 404 or 500, and the Semantic Scholar and arXiv APIs returned HTTP 429. Gap 3 stays open for page-level claims and for frog-story manner/path numbers by language and age.
limits: Lack of access, not lack of evidence.
agent_relevance: None; the founding numbers remain second-hand.

source: Qi, Chen, Xiong, Fernandez, Bitterman & Bisazza (2025) When Models Reason in Your Language: Controlling Thinking Language Comes at the Cost of Accuracy (arXiv 2505.22888)
finding: Six reasoning models (Distilled-R1 1.5B to 32B, Skywork-OR1 7B and 32B) were tested on XReasoning: AIME2024, AIME2025, GPQA and MGSM in 11 languages. By default models often fail to think in the question language. A prompt prefix forcing the thinking language lifts matching to about 98% but cuts accuracy, most on hard tasks.
numbers: Distill-R1-32B language matching 46.3% on AIME, 42.3% on GPQA, 94.0% on MGSM. Prompt hack raised matching from an average of 46% to 98% and cut accuracy from 26% to 17% on average. R1-32B accuracy AIME 25.5 to 17.0, GPQA 40.3 to 33.4, MGSM 70.2 to 71.7. Skywork-32B AIME 44.8 to 29.6. XReasoning has 370 questions.
limits: Prompt-hack forcing, not natural use. MGSM is easy so the effect is small there.
agent_relevance: Extends the penalty (gap 7) to AIME and GPQA, harder than MATH-500: forcing a non-English thinking language costs accuracy and the cost grows with difficulty. Do not force a thinking language in the scaffold.

source: Zhao, Liu, Schutze & Hedderich (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Multilingual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning (arXiv 2510.09555)
finding: Reasoning models told to think in the prompt language often do not (compliance under 0.2 for Bengali and Yoruba across all models). Prompt hacking gives very high compliance but lower final-answer accuracy, for example for Yoruba. Swapping thinking traces between languages shows traces are not consistent across languages, and answer accuracy depends on prompt language as well as thinking language. Non-English thinking depends more on the trace.
numbers: Compliance under 0.2 for bn and yo under explicit instruction; prompt hacking near full compliance. Per-cell accuracies in Table 1 of the paper were not copied.
limits: Abstract, setup and results prose read; table cells not extracted.
agent_relevance: Second paper, different authors, agrees with d09 on the control-versus-accuracy trade-off. Supports raising K10 from single-source.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Think Natively: Unlocking Multilingual Reasoning with Consistency-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning (M-Thinker, arXiv 2510.07300 v3)
finding: Existing reasoning models often fail to keep input, thinking and answer languages the same and score lower on non-English inputs. Training with GRPO using a language-consistency reward and a cross-lingual alignment reward (compare non-English reasoning with the model's own English reasoning) gives near 100% language consistency and better accuracy on MMATH and PolyMath for 1.5B, 4B and 7B models.
numbers: Abstract states nearly 100% language consistency; per-language table cells not copied.
limits: Training result, compared against SFT, prompt controls and soft-reward RL baselines. Only abstract, setup and baselines were read closely.
agent_relevance: The English-thinking default can be trained away without losing accuracy. The penalty in d09 is a property of current models, not of thinking in another language itself. Relevant to gap 6's training question.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Language as a Latent Variable for Reasoning Optimization (polyGRPO, arXiv 2604.21593)
finding: Polyglot Thinking Experiment on MGSM with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: for each question the response language was either constrained to one of 11 languages or left unconstrained. Chinese responses beat English on average; unconstrained was slightly below English-forced on average. They train polyGRPO from the contrast, using 18.1K math problems and no chain-of-thought labels.
numbers: Average MGSM accuracy by response language: en 64.22, zh 65.09, es 63.31, fr 63.24, ru 62.98, ja 60.65, de 60.55, th 57.38, sw 42.29, bn 39.45, te 19.42; unconstrained 63.16. English questions: en 81.2, zh 87.2, es 84.8, fr 84.0. polyGRPO +6.72 points over base on four English reasoning sets, +6.89 on the multilingual benchmark, +4.9 on English commonsense.
limits: One 7B model in the base experiment. The abstract says best performance often comes unconstrained, but the average for unconstrained (63.16) is below English-forced (64.22), so that claim is about per-cell results. Not equal-token for branches.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partial: on one open model a response language other than English can beat English for some questions (zh 87.2 vs en 81.2 on English questions), the premise for language-diverse branches. No test at equal total tokens with voting.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Less Languages, Less Tokens: UL-XCoT (arXiv 2604.20090)
finding: Cross-lingual chain-of-thought with self-consistency: sample reasoning in several languages and vote. UL-XCoT picks a few candidate languages per query and prunes weak paths early, using over 50% fewer decoding tokens than prior sampling baselines. A monolingual control with the same pruning (UL-CoT) isolates the effect of using several languages. Multi-language voting beat the monolingual control at every difficulty level.
numbers: PolyMath, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, 18 languages, AVG accuracy. Low: CoT 54.0, SC 66.8, AutoCap 80.9, UL-CoT 65.5, UL-XCoT 83.8. Medium: SC 25.5, UL-CoT 26.3, UL-XCoT 31.1. High: SC 11.2, UL-CoT 12.3, UL-XCoT 13.6. Top: SC 8.2, UL-CoT 9.4, UL-XCoT 10.6. MMLU-ProX-Lite 29 languages: CLSP 40.5 to UL-XCoT 43.6.
limits: Token budgets are not equal between arms (UL-XCoT is cheaper); AutoCap (another multi-language voter) also does very well on Low. One 7B distilled model. Measures correctness; output diversity as in a21 is not measured.
agent_relevance: Best evidence for gap 1: multi-language sampling plus voting beats the matched single-language control on correctness at lower token cost. Supports an optional multi-language branch step, but only tested on math with a small model.

source: Elhady, Agirre & Artetxe (2026) Cross-lingual Self-Consistency for Multilingual Reasoning with Language Models (arXiv 2606.01464); Soegeng et al. (2026) Cross-Lingual Consensus (arXiv 2605.22137)
finding: Two training-time uses of agreement across languages. Elhady et al. reward the same final answer for equivalent problems in different languages, with no gold answers or parallel data. Soegeng et al. use multilingual self-consistency to pick reliable cultural answers and transfer them to the weaker language.
numbers: Elhady: up to +21.7% average on MGSM over 10 languages, +18.2% mean on MGSM languages unseen in training, up to +6.2% on 3 out-of-distribution sets (Qwen2.5-Instruct 1.5B/7B/14B). Soegeng: +5.03% average on English queries in BLEnD, 16 regions.
limits: Both are training methods, not inference scaffolds. Abstract and setup read; not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Cross-language agreement is a usable signal. It needs a different setup before use as an inference-time branch-diversity step.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo & Griffiths (2024) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought Can Reduce Performance on Tasks Where Thinking Makes Humans Worse (arXiv 2410.21333)
finding: Closest LLM analogue found for gap 5. Tasks where humans do worse after verbalising (artificial grammar learning, face recognition after description, classification with exceptions) also lower model accuracy under chain-of-thought. Three tasks where verbal thinking hurts humans but not models are also reported, so the parallel is not exact.
numbers: Artificial grammar: o1-preview with reasoning 57.7% vs GPT-4o zero-shot 94.0% (36.3 points); GPT-4o 87.5% zero-shot vs 64.4% CoT; Claude 3 Opus 70.7% vs 62.7%. Face recognition after description: GPT-4o 64.0% vs 51.2%; Claude 3 Opus 44.0% vs 29.6%; Gemini 1.5 Pro 66.0% vs 54.6%; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8% vs 94.8%. InternVL2 26B 9.2% vs 6.0% (p=0.44).
limits: Not the Gennari design (describe first, then judge similarity by category), and not equal-token. Face recognition is a verbal overshadowing task, a different mechanism from event categories.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 only in part: a verbal step before a perceptual or implicit judgement can hurt. An agent should not run describe-first before pattern or perceptual judgements without a measured check.

source: Schut, Gal & Farquhar (2025) Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English? (arXiv 2502.15603), design comparison with Wendler et al. (2024)
finding: The authors say their work studies open-ended multi-token generation, in contrast to Wendler et al. (2024), whose single-token setting favoured a language-neutral concept space. English-close representations appear for content words (nouns), not for non-lexical words. Aya-23-35B is the least English-centric of four models and Gemma-2-27b the most. Steering vectors built in English work better than ones built in the output language.
numbers: Models: Aya-23-35B, Llama-3.1-70B, Mixtral-8x22B, Gemma-2-27b; languages English, French, German, Dutch, Mandarin. No single headline figure.
quote: prior work (Wendler et al., 2024) which found evidence for the second hypothesis in the single token context
limits: No reasoning-trained models were tested. The task-design explanation is the authors' own, not tested head to head.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly closed: disagreement is explained by task design (single token vs multi-token) and by model (English-centrism varies with the training mix, supported by Zhong et al., c07). Whether reasoning training changes it is open; d09 and d10 show reasoning models default to English thinking.

source: Wang, Qin & Liu (2026) Where Meanings Converge and Diverge: Revisiting Linguistic Relativity Across 81 Languages (arXiv 2610.30778)
finding: Using word embeddings from two multilingual encoders, relations among 196 basic concepts were compared across 81 languages. Socio-cultural concepts correspond more closely across languages than nature and motion concepts. Within the socio-cultural domain, dissimilarity grows with geographic distance.
numbers: 3,240 language pairs. Adjusted dissimilarity, mBERT: socio-cultural .874, nature and motion .924 (difference .0503, CrI .0470 to .0537). XLM-R-large: .922 vs .977 (difference .0547). Overall .910 (mBERT) and .932 (XLM-R). Nature and motion is 49 of the 196 concepts.
limits: Embeddings, not human judgements; the authors say this predicts but does not test human data. Absolute dissimilarities are high in every domain.
agent_relevance: Motion meanings differ more across languages in model space, consistent with motion being a domain where language-specific encoding matters. Background only.

source: Robertson, Roberts, Majid & Dunbar (2025) Language and economic behaviour: Future tense use causes less not more temporal discounting (PLoS One 20(5):e0317422)
finding: Boundary-condition case for grammar-to-cognition claims. A test of whether habitual future-tense use predicts discounting found the opposite sign to the usual cross-cultural story: English speakers using the future tense more discounted less.
numbers: Study 1 final n=235 (113 English, 122 Dutch). Bayesian mediation, 90% credibility intervals for one-tailed hypotheses.
limits: Not a motion or aspect paper. Study 2 details not extracted. It tests the future-tense hypothesis, not thinking for speaking.
agent_relevance: Grammar-driven cognition claims can reverse when tested at the individual-habit level. Weak support for caution in K07.

source: Search note: LLM and vision-language tests of manner/path, source-goal bias, describe-first (gaps 4, 5, 9)
finding: arXiv listing searches run this session ('motion events manner path', 'source-goal asymmetry language models', 'verbal overshadowing', 'Whorfian vision-language'; a long motion-event VLM query returned no results) found no paper that gives vision-language models motion clips in several languages and measures manner/path verb rates, none on source-goal bias in LLM-written plans, and none on describe-first steps in agents beyond d15. One web search also surfaced a CogSci semantics-guided action-understanding VLM paper (Xu, Wu, Tang, Hartshorne, Tenenbaum, Gao), seen only as a snippet and not about manner/path.
limits: Keyword search on arXiv listing pages is brittle. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv APIs were rate-limited. Not a proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 9 stay open. A direct test is cheap to design: same clips and prompts in several languages and a manner-verb rate per language.
